name: Generative rhythm: Euclidean patterns, polyrhythm, polymeter, probability and endless tempo illusions
goal: Generate rhythms and melodies algorithmically: Euclidean E(k,n) with rotation and boolean combinations, multi-layer scale weavers, polymeter lengths, probability/chance gates with seeds, constrained random sequencers, Risset accelerando and pendulum-wave phasing.

theory: E(k,n) spreads k hits as evenly as possible over n steps (E(3,8)=tresillo). Polyrhythm a:b = two pulse streams sharing a cycle; polymeter = loops of different lengths phasing. Probability with a fixed seed is repeatable.
prerequisites: Any generative or Euclidean step sequencer or DAW, or Polyrhythm Studio lanes / JS scheduler with scale quantiser, per-step random amounts, and a phrase reset (implementation note)
Any melodic synth or drum rack

DAW with a Euclidean generator script, or Web Audio / JS: up to 8 lanes, each a Bjorklund(pulses, steps) array rotated by its offset, mapped to scale[root + layerIndex] with per-lane velocity and gate (implementation note)

DAW with tempo automation and per-track volume automation, or Web Audio: a lookahead scheduler whose tempo ramps exponentially to 2× per cycle, with per-layer GainNode ramps and per-note velocity scaling for dropped subdivisions (implementation note)
Drum and bass voices; optional arpeggiator
Percussive or plucked voices, a sustained pad and a gliding voice

Sequencer with chance, Euclidean length and per-step random modulation (the video uses a small hardware synth), or Web Audio / JS: a step clock, a Bjorklund trigger mask of length 5 indexed mod 5 while notes are indexed mod 8, Math.random() gates, and scale quantising (implementation note)

Step sequencer or DAW/MIDI tool that can compute Euclidean patterns, or Web Audio / JS: compute Bjorklund patterns for two (pulses, length, rotation) sets and combine the boolean arrays per step (implementation note)
Synth voice with distortion, release, filter and wavetable position as modulation targets

outputs.description: Rendered part or recipe following the workflow

constraints: Portable recipe; not affiliated with any vendor; do not copy factory presets or sample packs.
Numbers in variants come from the source video transcripts; workflow steps are the consolidated mainstream practice.
Bring drums in early and avoid pitch wobble unless asked (user preferences from daily tests).

steps.action: Choose a grid (16ths) and base pattern E(k,n); rotate to move the accent.
Layer 2-8 Euclidean generators, each mapped to a drum or one scale note; combine with OR/XOR/AND for new patterns.
Set different loop lengths (e.g. 16 vs 12 vs 7 steps) for polymeter evolution.
Add chance rests, random octave/degree within scale, random accents; seed it so it's repeatable.
Tame: constrain to scale and 1-2 octaves, fewer pitches, phrase restart points, randomize only last notes.
Illusions: Risset rhythm (crossfaded doubling tempo layers), pendulum wave (lanes with slightly longer periods realign after N cycles).
Print to MIDI/steps and edit by ear.
Hear the theory: run `/home/box/audio-tools/bin/python sample-lab/theory/rhythm_polyrhythm.py` from the repo root and compare the sections; reuse its functions as a starting point for renders.
steps.expect: WAV in sample-lab/theory/out/ demonstrating the principle

verification: Render a short test and A/B against a reference at matched loudness
Run the generator and confirm it writes a WAV without error
Check mono compatibility and that no element masks the kick/bass

variants.name: Two Euclidean pulse generators per track combined with Boolean logic (OR, XOR, AND, SUB), per-generator rotation and whole-track rotation, then printed to an ordinary step sequence for hand edits; also used to redistribute an existing bassline and to leave gaps an arpeggiator fills
variants.goal: Generate musically coherent, non-obvious drum and melodic patterns by combining two Euclidean pulse generators on one track. Each generator spreads N pulses as evenly as possible over the track length (e.g. 16 or 32 steps); numbers that do not divide the length (5, 9, 11, 12) give the interesting grooves. Combine the two with a Boolean operator: OR (any pulse plays; overlaps become one note), XOR (overlaps are removed, leaving space), AND (only overlaps play; the number of possible notes is limited by the smaller pulse count) or SUB (generator 1 minus where it overlaps generator 2, a way to carve notes out). Rotate each generator to change their relationship, then rotate the whole track to move the downbeat of the combined pattern. Print the result to a normal step sequence to edit single notes, apply the same Euclidean distribution to a pre-programmed melodic line (notes stay, positions change), randomise the Euclidean settings with a snapshot to return to, and let an arpeggiator with step offsets fill the gaps. Delta beyond our probability/seeded loop skills: the two-generator Boolean combine plus print-to-steps workflow, mapped to Polyrhythm Studio lanes.
steps: Turn on Euclidean mode for a drum track. Set generator 1 to a simple count (e.g. 4 pulses over 16 steps) and listen; then try counts that do not divide 16 (5, 11).
Enable generator 2 with a different count (e.g. 5 against 4) using OR. Rotate generator 2 to move its hits against generator 1.

Switch the operator: XOR to remove overlapping hits and open space; AND to keep only overlaps (raise counts, e.g. 9 and 12, and rotate until notes appear); SUB to keep generator 1 except where generator 2 lands.
When an emergent pattern makes a new downbeat, use whole-track rotation (e.g. +3 steps) to move both generators together so that hit becomes step 1.
Print the pattern to the normal step sequencer, then hand-edit (move a note, leave room for a snare). Build hats on another track at length 32 with SUB to carve notes out of a dense generator 1.

On a melodic (bass) track with notes already programmed, enable Euclidean mode so those notes are redistributed by the pulse pattern; add generator 2 with XOR and rotate the track. Randomise the Euclidean settings repeatedly until a version works.
For sparse patterns, enable an arpeggiator and remove one arp note with its offset/step mask so it fills gaps without crowding.
For performance, change rotations and pulses on all tracks at once, and keep a snapshot so you can jump back to the original pattern.

variants.name: Eight-layer Euclidean pattern generator with two modes: drums (each layer = one MIDI drum note) and melody (each layer = a different note of a chosen scale and root, so stacked layers form in-key chords); per-layer steps, pulses, rotation, velocity and gate, a drift action that nudges each layer's pulses by ±1, layer or global randomise that never changes note assignment, and scale/root changes that keep the rhythm
variants.goal: Write in-key polyrhythmic melodies and grooves by stacking up to eight Euclidean layers. Each layer has steps (pattern length), pulses (hits spread as evenly as possible), rotation (offset, which shifts layers against each other), velocity and gate (note length). In drum mode each layer triggers its own drum note; in melody mode each layer is assigned a different note from a chosen scale and root, so layers of different lengths interlock into melodies and coinciding hits make chords, always in key. Generate the result into a clip, add layers one at a time, use drift to randomly move each active layer's pulse count up or down by one, and randomise a layer or everything except the note assignment. Keep a rhythm you like and change scale (e.g. to Phrygian) or root afterwards. Shorten gate if notes are too long. For Polyrhythm Studio: one Euclidean lane per scale degree with independent lengths.
steps: Choose drum mode and assign layers to drum notes (kick, snare, closed hat, etc.). Enable two layers, set steps/pulses/rotation, and generate.
Add layers one at a time (e.g. closed hat, crash), set each layer's velocity and gate, and regenerate.
Change a layer's rotation or pulses (e.g. move the snare), or press randomise for one layer; use drift to move every active layer's pulse count by ±1.
Switch to melody mode, choose scale and root. Each layer now plays a different scale note; enable several layers with different step lengths.
Shorten gate if notes overlap too much; randomise all (notes stay fixed) until a rhythm works.
Keep the rhythm and change the scale or root (e.g. to Phrygian) and regenerate.

variants.name: Generative rhythmic sequence from a hand-written 8-step pattern: live length and start-point changes, chance-based rests, a 5-step Euclidean trigger length phasing against the 8 steps (a 40-step cycle), random modulation of octave and scale degree kept subtle, random distortion and release for accents and note lengths, smooth-random slow LFOs on filter and wavetable position, introduced gradually in performance
variants.goal: Turn a short, intentional sequence into an evolving techno or ambient line without writing new notes. Start from a programmed 8-step pattern (or, for pure random, a one-step root note with random → scale degree attenuated to about 7–8 degrees, which gives quantised random melodies within one octave). Vary it by changing pattern length and start point while it plays. Add rests with chance (about 75% means roughly one in four steps silent) and/or a Euclidean trigger length that does not divide the step count (5 against 8): with chance slightly under 100% (about 90%) the 5-step trigger pattern shifts across the 8 notes and the cycle repeats only after 40 steps. Add a tempo-synced delay so echoes fill the rests. Then add pitch variation by patching random to octave (positive for up, negative for down jumps) and to scale degree (jumps of about 4–5 degrees), keeping both subtle so the line's shape survives. Add sound variation: random → distortion (accents) and random → release (note lengths, with a lower base release), and slow smooth-random LFOs (around 5 s) on filter cutoff and wavetable position. Don't use everything at once; bring modulations in gradually across a set.
steps: Program an 8-step sequence (or one root step plus random → scale degree around 7–8 degrees for an instant quantised random melody). Save it as the base.
While playing, change pattern length and set a different start point to get variation from the same notes (e.g. steps 1–16 vs 17–32 for different song sections).
Set chance to about 75% for random rests. Alternatively set a Euclidean trigger length of 5 with chance about 90%, so the 5-step trigger pattern drifts across the 8 notes.
Add a tempo-synced delay so echoes land in the rests.

Patch random → octave (positive = up jumps, negative = down) and random → scale degree, attenuating until jumps of about 4–5 degrees appear. Optionally map degree to a knob to sweep between bassline and lead register.
Patch random → distortion for accents and random → release for varied note lengths; lower the base release so variation is audible.
Add LFO X (smooth random, slow) → filter cutoff and LFO Y (smooth random, about 5 s) → wavetable position, with base position above zero.
When performing, start with the plain sequence and introduce degree, octave and timbre modulation one by one over time.

variants.name: Pendulum-wave arpeggio (measured from Virtual Riot "Pendulum Sequence 2"): one repeating short note per scale lane, lanes slightly slower going down, so the figure drifts into staircases and curves and realigns after ~408 cycles
steps: 1. Set the tempo to 30 BPM. Make 35 lanes, E8 at the top down to E1, using E minor without C (thinning in the low register).
2. The top lane plays a note every 1/2 beat. Lane i plays at frequency f0·(N−i)/N, with N = 408; that is about +0.245 % period per lane, so the bottom lane is ×1.083 slower.
3. Note length is 0.37 × the lane's own period. All lanes start at the same moment; the staircase comes from the drift.
4. Voice: a 3-saw stack, lowpass at about 2.4 kHz, fast attack, exponential decay, top lanes a few dB quieter.
5. Stack 10 copies with about ±7 cents of detune, about ±9 ms of offset, and panning spread; add a short cross-delay. Target −15 LUFS, about −4 dBTP and side about −11 dB.
6. Arrange it as: sparse intro (every 3rd lane), full phasing, a realign moment (start the pattern N·period − x seconds in so the realign lands where you want it), then an outro.

variants.name: Endless-accelerando (Risset rhythm) illusion for cinematic tension: the same pattern at double speed fading out and at half speed fading in while tempo automates to double, dropped subdivisions (fade every other note of a six-pulse group as tempo doubles), half-speed (3/4) and third-speed (6/8) copies forming a 3:2 hemiola fractal, voices swapping roles across cycles, and a long note gliding slowly against a sustained pitch
variants.goal: Make a rhythm that seems to speed up forever without ever getting too fast, the rhythmic version of a Shepard tone. Basic form: play a pattern, the same pattern at double speed fading out above it, and at half speed fading in below it, while tempo automates up to double; then loop. In a track: take a group of six steady pulses and, as tempo rises toward double, fade every second note until it disappears, so at double tempo you hear the original rhythm again. Layer the same six-pulse pattern at half speed (three strong pulses, 3/4 feel) and at one-third speed (two pulses, 6/8 feel) for a 3:2 hemiola; give each layer its own dropped-subdivision transformation and fade layers in and out across cycles so the ear never locks onto one, and let a voice that played the 2-pulse role take the 3-pulse role in the next cycle. Double tempo per cycle (150 → 300 → 600 in the video) and reset where the DAW tempo ceiling is reached. Add tension with a long note rising slowly against a sustained pitch, passing every dissonance. Fits Polyrhythm Studio as tempo-scaled lanes with per-lane gain automation.
steps: Build the basic form: one pattern, a double-speed copy fading out over the cycle, a half-speed copy fading in, and tempo automated to double over the same cycle. Loop it.
Dropped subdivisions: play a group of six pulses; as tempo rises toward double, ramp down the level of every second note until silent.
Add the same six-pulse pattern at half speed (three strong pulses, 3/4 feel) and at one-third speed (two pulses, 6/8 feel).

Apply the dropped-subdivision fade to each layer in turn, staggering them, and fade whole layers in and out across cycles; let a voice move from the 2-pulse role to the 3-pulse role in the next section.
Automate tempo doubling cycle by cycle (e.g. 150 → 300 → 600) and reset to the start tempo at a cycle boundary when you hit the tempo ceiling, with fades placed in those transition zones.
Add tension: a long note gliding slowly upward against a sustained pitch, plus heavily reverberated vocal or texture layers.

variants.name: Three rules for making a randomised/Euclidean sequencer sound intentional: constrain (scale, octave range, pitches pulled close, phrase length), repeat (global randomness to zero, reset per-step random, restart points so the phrase retriggers each bar), and simplify (about three pitches, fewer pulses, complexity from layering simple parts), then add hand-made variations on chosen cycles and random pitch options on only the last few notes
variants.goal: Fix a generative patch that sounds aimlessly random. Rule 1, constrain: set a scale (e.g. minor), reduce octave range/voicing, and pull spread-out notes into closer octaves; limit phrase length. Rule 2, repetition creates anticipation: turn global continuous randomisation to zero, reset any per-step randomisation (use only a little, on a couple of notes), and set a restart point so the pitch and trigger lists start together each bar, so the ear can remember the hook. Rule 3, less is more: cut to about three pitches and fewer pulses; get complexity from several simple layers, not one complex one. Then add intentional variation: in a later cycle (e.g. bar 2) add extra notes, copy that variation to other cycles, move start points, push one note up an octave or add a roll; for controlled surprise, give only the last four notes extra pitch options. Apply the same rules to each part. Complements our probability/seeded generative skills as the taming pass.
steps: Solo one part. Set a scale, reduce octave range, and move notes into nearby octaves.
Set global continuous randomisation to zero and reset per-step random amounts on all steps.
Add a restart point so pitch and trigger cycles realign at the start of every bar.
Reduce to about three pitches and fewer pulses; optionally add a second restart point.
Pick a cycle (e.g. bar 2) and hand-add notes; copy that variation to other cycles, change start points, raise one note an octave, add a roll.
Give only the last few notes (e.g. last four) extra pitch options or randomisation.
Repeat rules 1–3 for each other part and listen to them together.
